sourceInformation.source: Keystone Kapers (Activision, 1983), designed by Garry Kitchen
sourceInformation.tech: Three.js 0.180.0 (R180), WebGPURenderer; Rapier 3D 0.19.3; Gamepad API; Web Audio; PeerJS 1.5.5; AI Hub Session Protocol v1 client 1.4.0
sourceInformation.artDirection: Procedural cel-shaded meshes, ink outlines, Art Deco department store, cream / teal / brass palette
sourceInformation.animation: Three.js AnimationMixer / AnimationClip and keyframe tracks; procedural prop, lift, escalator and particle animation
sourceInformation.audio: Original code-generated ragtime, synthesized Foley and Animalese-style gibberish; music defaults to 10%; no audio files
sourceInformation.online: 1–4 player host-authoritative online co-op with PeerJS; same-origin local-tab transport; AI Hub shared-world sessions; 1–2 couch co-op
sourceInformation.testing: Headless Chromium WebGPU, scripted whole-game playthrough, physics and game-state checks, emulated standard gamepad, touch profile, offline audio render, two-page networking and official AI Hub harness; screenshots for visual review
sourceInformation.research: Original Activision manual, 1983 advertising, Atari/Atarimania imagery and source sound descriptions; official Three.js, Rapier and AI Hub documentation

testingFeedback: 8 confirmed issues caught and fixed across automated tests and visual review.
2 game-breaking issues: a Rapier startup API mismatch and incorrect seat assignment for three/four-player local-tab rooms.
The complete three-case playthrough with actual Rapier physics, default tuning, active hazards and the finale lift shortcut.
Headless WebGPU screenshots were blank on this adapter; state assertions and WebGL fallback captures were more useful.
engineFeedback: Native AnimationMixer clips and WebGPU toon materials made the procedural cast expressive and cohesive.
I initially used live-body setter names on a Rapier body descriptor. Actual-version tests caught the mismatch. Headless WebGPU image capture also required a WebGL visual fallback.
The floor-aware chase simulation, cycling lift and escalators, controller menu focus, procedural audio and authoritative co-op snapshots.
Coordinating fixed-step physics, native animation, menu focus and asynchronous multiplayer state in a single-file release.
Dependable headless WebGPU screenshot/readback support across software adapters.
promptFeedback: Researching the original and designing for a TV controller gave the game a clear identity and useful constraints.
The target length of a feature-complete demo and the desired multiplayer player count were unspecified.
Completing and validating gameplay, every input method, synthesized audio, standalone networking and Hub sessions as one portable HTML.
Specify a target demo duration and player count while keeping the source-research and vertical-slice requirements.

aiHub.name: Keystone Caper Cart
aiHub.tagline: One crook. Four floors. Absolutely no running.
aiHub.description: Clock in as Officer Pip for a slapstick chase through the Grand Keystone Emporium. Jump runaway carts, duck toy planes, recover the takings and use the lift to corner Sid Slip across three escalating cases, solo or with a co-op patrol.
aiHub.controls: Left stick/D-pad or A/D: move; Cross/A or Space: jump; Circle/B or S: duck; Square/X or E: cuff/lift; Up: lift; Options/Esc: pause. Touch: drag left, tap right, assisted evasion/cuffs. Couch P2: arrows, Right Ctrl, Enter.
